blurb: How Legionella grows in warm, still water, and the flushing, temperature and reporting habits that keep our water safe.

cards.title: Legionella & Water Hygiene Awareness
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- explain how Legionnaires' disease is caught
- keep water hot, cold and moving
- report warning signs to maintenance

cards.title: Water safety in a hotel
cards.body: With showers, taps and a hot tub, we have to take water hygiene seriously. Legionella bacteria live in water systems and can cause Legionnaires' disease, a serious, sometimes fatal, form of pneumonia.

cards.title: Breathed in, not drunk
cards.body: People catch it by breathing in tiny water droplets, a fine spray or mist, from things like showers, taps and spa pools. They do not catch it by drinking the water.

cards.title: Warm, still, scaled-up water
cards.body: Legionella thrives in warm, stagnant water, roughly between 20°C and 45°C, and where there is scale, rust or sludge to feed on.

cards.title: Temperature and moving water
cards.body: We keep it in check by controlling temperature and keeping water moving.

items.title: Outlets
items.text: Used regularly so water does not sit still.

cards.title: Flush little-used outlets
cards.body:
If a room, tap or shower has not been used for a while, it must be flushed through before a guest uses it. Run the water to clear stagnant water in the pipes.

Keep showerheads and taps clean and descaled. Scale gives bacteria somewhere to grow.

items.title: Check last use
items.text: Has it been unused for a while?

items.title: Flush through
items.text: Run the water to clear the pipes.

cards.title: Spot the warning signs
cards.body: You do not need to be a specialist, but you do need to report the warning signs to maintenance so they can be checked.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Legionella is caught by breathing in droplets, not drinking
- It thrives in warm, still water roughly between 20°C and 45°C
- Hot above 50°C, cold below 20°C, and keep water moving
- Flush little-used outlets before a guest uses them
- Report warning signs to maintenance

cards.q: Legionnaires' disease is caught by breathing in tiny water droplets, not by drinking water.
cards.why: The risk comes from fine spray or mist from showers, taps and spa pools.

cards.q: Legionella thrives in water that is:
cards.why: It thrives in warm, stagnant water, and where scale, rust or sludge feeds it.

cards.q: A bedroom has been empty for a while. What must you do to its shower and taps before a guest uses them?
options: Flush through to clear stagnant water
Wipe the showerhead and leave it
Just turn it on to check it works
Leave it until the guest reports a problem
cards.why: Run the water to clear stagnant water sitting in the pipes before a guest uses it.

cards.q: Hot water should be kept properly hot (above 50°C) and cold water genuinely cold (below 20°C).
cards.why: Controlling temperature is how we keep Legionella in check.

cards.q: Legionnaires' disease is a serious form of:
cards.why: It is a serious, sometimes fatal, form of pneumonia.

cards.q: Scale on a showerhead gives bacteria somewhere to grow.
cards.why: Keep showerheads and taps clean and descaled.

cards.q: Which is a warning sign you should report to maintenance?
options: A tap that drips a little
A shower that is slow to heat
Hot water that is only lukewarm
cards.why: Report cold water running warm, hot water only lukewarm, scaled showerheads or unused outlets.

cards.q: Keeping water moving (using outlets regularly) helps control Legionella.
cards.why: Outlets used regularly means water does not sit still.

cards.q: Because we have a hot tub, showers and taps, water hygiene matters here.
cards.why: With showers, taps and a hot tub, we have to take water hygiene seriously.
